definitions.text: To remove the face or cover from; to unmask; to expose.
Infallible. [Obs.] "This unfailable word of truth." Bp. Hall.
Not failing; not liable to fail; inexhaustible; certain; sure.
To deprive of fairness or beauty. [R.] Shak.
Not fair; not honest; not impartial; disingenuous; using or involving trick or artifice; dishonest; unjust; unequal. You come, like an unfair merchant, to charge me with being in your
Absence or want of faith; faithlessness; distrust; unbelief. [R.] Faith and unfaith can ne'er be equal powers: Unfaith in aught is want of faith in all. Tennyson.

Not faithful; not observant of promises, vows, allegiance, or duty; violating trust or confidence; treacherous; perfidious; as, an unfaithful subject; an unfaithful agent or servant. My feet, through wine, unfaithful to their weight. Pope. His honor rooted in dishonor stood, And faith unfaithful kept him falsely true. Tennyson.
Not possessing faith; infidel. [R.] Milton.
Not falcated, or hooked.
Having no deductions; not curtailed, or shortened; undiminished. [R.] Swift.
Infallible. Shak.
To loose; to unfix; to unbind; to untie.
Having no father; fatherless; hence, born contrary to nature. Shak.
Having no acknowledged father; hence, illegitimate; spurious; bastard.
To deprive of feathers; to strip. [R.]
Wanting regular features; deformed. "Visage rough, deformed, unfeatured, and a skin of buff." Dryden.
Not feat; not dexterous; unskillful; clumsy. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.
Destitute of feeling; void of sensibility; insensible; insensate.
Without kind feelings; cruel; hard-hearted. To each his sufferings: all are men, Condemned alike to groan; The
Not feigned; not counterfeit; not hypocritical; real; sincere; genuine; as, unfeigned piety; unfeigned love to man. "Good faith unfeigned." Chaucer.
To prevent from being a fellow or companion; to separate from one's fellows; to dissever. Death quite unfellows us. Mrs. Browning.
Being without a fellow; unmatched; unmated. Shak.
To strip of a fence; to remove a fence from.
Unfit for a feast; hence, jaded; worn. [Obs.] Chaucer.
To loose from fetters or from restraint; to unchain; to unshackle; to liberate; as, to unfetter the mind.
To free from feudal customs or character; to make not feudal. Carlyle.
To remove from a file or record.
Not defiled; pure. [Obs.] Surrey.
Unsuitable to a son or a daughter; undutiful; not becoming a
Not finished, not brought to an end; imperfect; incomplete; left in the rough; wanting the last hand or touch; as, an unfinished house; an unfinished picture; an unfinished iron casting.
Infirm. [R.] Dryden.
Infirmness. [R.]

To make unsuitable or incompetent; to deprive of the strength, skill, or proper qualities for anything; to disable; to incapacitate; to disqualify; as, sickness unfits a man for labor; sin unfits us for the society of holy beings.
To loosen from a fastening; to detach from anything that holds; to unsettle; as, to unfix a bayonet; to unfix the mind or affections.
To make fluid; to dissolve. [R.] The mountain stands; nor can the rising sun Unfix her frosts. Dryden.
Not fledged; not feathered; hence, not fully developed; immature. Dryden.
To deprive of flesh; to reduce a skeleton. "Unfleshed humanity." Wordsworth.
Not pertaining to the flesh; spiritual.
Inflexible.
To strip of flowers. [R.] G. Fletcher.
To open the folds of; to expand; to spread out; as, to unfold a tablecloth. Unfold thy forehead gathered into frowns. Herbert.

To open, as anything covered or close; to lay open to view or contemplation; to bring out in all the details, or by successive development; to display; to disclose; to reveal; to elucidate; to explain; as, to unfold one's designs; to unfold the principles of a science. Unfold the passion of my love. Shak.
To release from a fold or pen; as, to unfold sheep.
To open; to expand; to become disclosed or developed. The wind blows cold While the morning doth unfold. J. Fletcher.
One who, or that which, unfolds.
The acct of unfolding, or the state of being unfolded. The extreme unfoldment of the instinctive powers. C. Morris.
To restore from folly, or from being a fool. [Obs.] Shak.
To fail to foresee. Bp. Hacket.
Incapable of being foreseen. South.
Deprived of the foreskin; circumcised. [R.] Milton.
Not forgettable; enduring in memory. Pungent and unforgettable truths. Emerson.
To decompose, or resolve into parts; to destroy the form of; to unmake. [R.] Good.
Decomposed, or resolved into parts; having the form destroyed.
Not formed; not arranged into regular shape, order, or relations; shapeless; amorphous.
(Biol.)
Unorganized; without definite shape or structure; as, an unformed, or unorganized, ferment. Unformed stars (Astron.), stars not grouped into any constellation; informed stars. See Sporades.
Not fortunate; unsuccessful; not prosperous; unlucky; attended with misfortune; unhappy; as, an unfortunate adventure; an unfortunate man; an unfortunate commander; unfortunate business.
Not founded; not built or established. Milton.
Having no foundation; baseless; vain; idle; as, unfounded expectations. Paley.
To take apart, or destroy the frame of. Dryden.
Infrangible. [Obs.] "Impassible and unfrangible." Jer. Taylor.
Not frankable; incapable of being sent free by public conveyance.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + fraught.]
Not fraught; not burdened.
Etym: [1st pref. un- + fraught.]
Removed, as a burden; unloaded. P. Fletcher.
Not free; held in bondage. There had always been a slave class, a class of the unfree, among the English as among all German peoples. J. R. Green
To thaw. [Obs.]
Infrequency.
Infrequent. J. H. Newman.
To cease to frequent. [Obs.] They quit their thefts and unfrequent the fields. J. Philips.
Rarely visited; seldom or never resorted to by human beings; as, an unfrequented place or forest. Addison.
To smooth after being fretted. [Obs.]
One not a friend; an enemy. [R.] Carlyle.
Wanting friends; not befriended; not countenanced or supported. Goldsmith. If Richard indeed does come back, it must be alone, unfollowed, unfriended. Sir W. Scott.
Not friendly; not kind or benevolent; hostile; as, an unfriendly neighbor.
Not favorable; not adapted to promote or support any object; as,
The state or quality of being unfriendly; unfriendliness; enmity. An act of unfriendship to my sovereign person. Sir W. Scott.
To deprive or divest or a frock; specifically, to deprive of priestly character or privilege; as, to unfrock a priest.
Not producing fruit or offspring; unproductive; infertile; barren; sterile; as, an unfruitful tree or animal; unfruitful soil;
Not exposed to fumes; not fumigated. Milton.
To loose from a furled state; to unfold; to expand; to open or spread; as, to unfurl sails; to unfurl a flag.
To strip of furniture; to divest; to strip.
Infusible. [R.]
